text: The Liturgy of Addai and Mari is the main eucharistic liturgy of the East Syriac tradition. It is named after Addai and Mari, the missionaries traditionally credited with evangelising Edessa and Mesopotamia. Its anonymous core anaphora is usually dated to the third century or later, and the whole rite took shape over several centuries. It is one of the oldest eucharistic prayers still in use and is notable because its manuscripts lack an explicit narrative of institution. The Assyrian Church of the East, the Chaldean Catholic Church and the Syro-Malabar Church all still use it.

"On the Beginning of Creation" is the opening sermon of the first series of Catholic Homilies, the Old English collection that Ælfric of Eynsham compiled around 989–991 for preaching through the church year. Its rubric says it may be preached to the people at any time. It sets out basic Christian teaching: God as the one origin of all things, the Trinity, the creation and orders of angels, and the fall of the rebellious angels. It then turns to the creation and fall of humankind and gives a short account of sacred history, introducing the whole series.

This Old English sermon for Christmas Day (25 December) is the second homily in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham. He compiled the series around 989–991 as a set of vernacular preaching texts for the church year. Ælfric retells the Nativity from Luke's Gospel, including the census, the birth at Bethlehem and the angel's message to the shepherds, and then explains its meaning for his listeners. He draws on Latin patristic interpretation to teach that Christ was born truly human while remaining divine. It is a key example of late Anglo-Saxon preaching in English.

This Old English homily for the feast of Saint Stephen on 26 December is the third item in the first series of the Catholic Homilies. Ælfric of Eynsham wrote the series around 989–991. Drawing on the Acts of the Apostles, it tells how the apostles ordained seven deacons, with Stephen first among them. It goes on to describe his miracles, the false charges brought against him, his speech before the Jewish council and his stoning as the first Christian martyr. It is part of Ælfric's yearly cycle of sermons, written to give clear teaching in English.

This Old English homily for 27 December, the feast of John the Evangelist, is the fourth piece in the first series of Catholic Homilies. Ælfric of Eynsham wrote the series around 989–991. Drawing on Latin legends about the apostle, it presents John as Christ's beloved disciple and cousin, chosen for his virginity. It follows a tradition that he was the bridegroom at Cana and left his bride to follow Christ. It then tells how Christ entrusted Mary to him, how he survived Domitian's vat of boiling oil, and of his later miracles and his peaceful passing.

This Old English homily for the feast of the Holy Innocents on 28 December is the fifth item in the first series of Ælfric of Eynsham's Catholic Homilies, composed around 989–991. The Latin title Natale Innocentium uses natale in its liturgical sense of a martyr's feast day, or "heavenly birthday". The homily retells the account in Matthew's Gospel of the Magi's visit and Herod's massacre of the children of Bethlehem, then explains it for a lay audience. It honours the infants as the first martyrs for Christ.

This is an Old English sermon for 1 January, the sixth item in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, written around 989–991. It explains Luke's brief account of Christ's circumcision and naming on the eighth day. Ælfric traces circumcision back to God's covenant with Abraham and interprets the rite spiritually as the cutting away of sin. Like the rest of the collection, it brings patristic exegesis to a lay audience in clear vernacular prose, as part of the Benedictine reform in late Anglo-Saxon England.

This Old English sermon for the feast of the Epiphany (6 January) is the seventh homily in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, written around 989–991. It returns to the Gospel of Matthew's account of the Magi, which had already been read a few days earlier. Ælfric explains the feast as Christ's manifestation to the three kings, at his baptism and at the wedding at Cana. He then interprets the Magi's journey and their gifts. Drawing on patristic commentary, it shows how Ælfric made Latin learning available to lay audiences in English.

This Old English sermon is the eighth homily in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, the Benedictine monk and homilist. It was written around 990 and is meant for the Third Sunday after Epiphany. It explains the Gospel reading from Matthew 8, in which Jesus comes down from the mountain and heals a leper. Following the Carolingian commentator Haymo, Ælfric reads the passage allegorically. The mountain stands for heaven, and Christ's descent for the Incarnation. The crowd that follows him stands for faithful Christians who imitate Christ through good works.

This Old English sermon by Ælfric of Eynsham is the ninth homily in the first series of his Catholic Homilies, written around 989–991. It was meant for the feast of the Purification of the Virgin Mary on 2 February, also called Candlemas. It starts from the Gospel account in Luke 2. First it explains the Mosaic law on purification after childbirth. Then it tells of the presentation of Christ in the Temple and Simeon's recognition of him. Like the rest of the collection, it was written to give clergy and lay people orthodox teaching in the vernacular.

This is the tenth homily in the first series of the Catholic Homilies, the Old English sermon collection that the Benedictine monk Ælfric of Eynsham wrote around 990. It was meant for Quinquagesima, the Sunday before Lent, and explains the gospel of the day, Luke 18:31–43. In that passage Christ foretells his Passion and heals a blind man near Jericho. Following Gregory the Great, Ælfric reads the blind man as fallen mankind enlightened by Christ. He also urges his hearers to faith, persistent prayer and good works as they prepare for the Lenten fast.

This Old English sermon for the First Sunday in Lent is the eleventh homily in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, completed around 989–991. It first retells the gospel account of Christ's temptation in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11) in English. It then explains the passage, drawing on patristic exegesis, especially Gregory the Great. Ælfric discusses Christ's forty-day fast, the devil's three temptations and how they are overcome, and the Lenten duties of fasting, almsgiving and repentance.

This Old English sermon by Ælfric of Eynsham is the twelfth homily in the first series of his Catholic Homilies, which he compiled around 989–991. It was written for the fourth Sunday of Lent, known as Midlent Sunday. The homily retells the Gospel reading of the day, John 6:1–14, in which Jesus feeds five thousand people with five barley loaves and two fishes. Ælfric then explains the miracle and its spiritual meaning, following Augustine's commentary on John. He wrote the homily to teach lay people in their own language.

This Old English sermon for the feast of the Annunciation on 25 March is the thirteenth homily in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, written around 989–991. It explains Luke's account of Gabriel's message to Mary. Ælfric sets it within salvation history, from creation and the devil's fall to Adam's sin and the prophecies of redemption, including Isaiah's virgin oracle. He then explains the Incarnation and praises Mary's virginity and humility for a lay audience.

This Old English sermon for Palm Sunday is the fourteenth homily in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham. The series was compiled around 989–991. The sermon was meant to be preached after the reading of the Passion. It retells Christ's entry into Jerusalem, set against the raising of Lazarus, and then explains the passage allegorically. The two disciples sent to fetch the ass stand for the teachers God sends to instruct mankind. Ælfric drew on earlier Latin commentators to give English congregations patristic biblical interpretation in their own language.

This Old English homily for Easter Day is the fifteenth piece in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, a Benedictine monk. The series was compiled around 989–991. Ælfric reminds his congregation of Christ's resurrection. He retells the guarding of the tomb, rejects the claim that the body was stolen, and recounts the appearances to the disciples up to the Ascension. He then expounds the day's gospel. The homily shows how Ælfric brought patristic exegesis to lay audiences in the vernacular.

This is an Old English sermon for the first Sunday after Easter, the sixteenth item in the first series of the Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, written around 990. It explains the Gospel reading from John 20, in which the risen Christ comes to his disciples through closed doors and Thomas touches his wounds. Ælfric relies mainly on Gregory the Great's homily on the same passage. He compares Christ's entry through shut doors with his birth from the Virgin, and explains how the resurrected body could be touched.

This Old English sermon by Ælfric of Eynsham belongs to the first series of his Catholic Homilies, written around 989–991. Composed for the Second Sunday after Easter, it explains the Gospel reading of the Good Shepherd (John 10:11–16). Christ is the good shepherd who gives his life for his sheep, and the apostles were good shepherds only through him as their head. Bishops and teachers are told to guard their people against the wolf, who is the devil, and not to flee like the hireling. Like much of the series, it draws on Gregory the Great's Gospel homilies.

This is an Old English sermon by Ælfric of Eynsham, the eighteenth homily in the first series of his Catholic Homilies, written around 989–991. It was meant for the litany or "prayer-days" of Rogationtide, when the faithful prayed for good harvests, health, peace and forgiveness of sins. Ælfric traces the custom to the three-day fast that Bishop Mamertus of Vienne ordered after earthquakes, wild beasts and fire struck his city. He links it to the repentance of Nineveh and retells the story of Jonah to urge penitence and prayer.

This Old English homily on the Lord's Prayer is the nineteenth item in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, the Benedictine monk and writer. The series was composed around 989 to 991. Meant for a Tuesday in Rogationtide, it first tells how Christ taught the apostles to pray. It then explains the Pater noster petition by petition, with teaching on God's fatherhood and Christians as adopted sons. It is a clear example of Ælfric's teaching aimed at lay people in their own language.

"Of the Catholic Faith" (De Fide Catholica) is an Old English homily by Ælfric of Eynsham, the twentieth item in the first series of his Catholic Homilies, composed around 989–991. It is assigned to a Wednesday, during Rogationtide, and follows directly on his sermon on the Lord's Prayer. In it Ælfric explains the Creed for lay listeners and presents the doctrine of the Trinity, drawing on Augustine. He starts from the distinction between the uncreated Creator and his creatures. The homily shows how the Benedictine reform tried to teach the basic points of faith in the vernacular.

This Old English sermon for the feast of the Ascension is the twenty-first item in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham. He compiled the series around 989–991 to provide orthodox preaching in the vernacular for the church year. The homily opens with a paraphrase of the liturgical reading from Acts 1. It retells Christ's forty days with his disciples after the resurrection, his promise of the Holy Spirit and his ascent from the Mount of Olives. It then explains the passage for a lay audience, drawing on earlier Latin patristic interpretation.

This Old English sermon for Pentecost is the twenty-second homily in the first series of the Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, written about 989–991. Ælfric explains how the feast began in the Old Testament. Israel kept Passover after the Exodus and the crossing of the Red Sea, and fifty days later God gave the Law at Sinai. He then sets this beside the Holy Spirit's descent on the apostles, as told in Acts. Like the rest of the series, it was meant to teach orthodox doctrine in English to lay listeners.

This Old English sermon is the twenty-third homily in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, written around 989–991. It was composed for the Second Sunday after Pentecost and explains the gospel parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31). Ælfric follows the exposition of Pope Gregory the Great and stresses that the rich man was condemned for meanness and pride rather than for theft. He warns against vanity in costly clothing and urges charity to the poor. The homily shows how Ælfric adapted patristic exegesis for preaching to lay audiences.

This Old English sermon by Ælfric of Eynsham is the twenty-fourth piece in the First Series of his Catholic Homilies, written around 989–991 and meant to be preached on the Fourth Sunday after Pentecost. It explains the Gospel reading from Luke 15, in which Pharisees and scribes complain that Jesus receives sinners, and he answers with the parable of the lost sheep. Ælfric openly follows Gregory the Great's interpretation. He reads the hundred sheep as angels and humankind, and the lost sheep as Adam, whom Christ came to earth to seek.

This Old English homily for the feast of the Nativity of John the Baptist on 24 June is the twenty-fifth item in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, compiled around 989–991. It explains the Gospel of Luke's account of the birth of John to Zacharias and Elizabeth and describes his ascetic life and his preaching in the wilderness. It also separates John's baptism, which did not forgive sins, from the baptism of Christ that he foretold. In this way Ælfric brought Latin patristic biblical interpretation to an English-speaking audience.

This Old English homily for the feast of Saints Peter and Paul on 29 June is the twenty-sixth item in the first series of Catholic Homilies. Ælfric of Eynsham wrote it around 989–991. It begins with an exposition of Matthew 16:13–19, which covers Peter's confession of Christ at Caesarea Philippi and the promise of the keys, drawing on Bede's commentary. It then tells the story of the two apostles' martyrdom at Rome. The homily is an example of Ælfric's effort to give lay audiences orthodox teaching in English, based on Latin patristic authorities.

This Old English homily by Ælfric of Eynsham was written for 30 June, the feast honouring the Apostle Paul. It is the twenty-seventh piece in the first series of his Catholic Homilies, composed around 989–991. The sermon retells Paul's life, drawing mainly on the Acts of the Apostles. It covers his early training in the Jewish law, his persecution of Christians and his part in Stephen's death, his conversion on the road to Damascus, and his martyrdom alongside Peter. Ælfric presents Paul as the teacher of all nations.

This Old English sermon belongs to the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, written about 989–991. It was meant to be preached on the Eleventh Sunday after Pentecost and explains the Gospel reading in which Jesus weeps over Jerusalem as he approaches the city (Luke 19:41 and following). Ælfric follows Gregory the Great's interpretation. He tells how the city's inhabitants rejected repentance, persecuted the apostles and were finally destroyed by the Romans under Vespasian. He presents that destruction as divine judgement and as a warning to the soul.

This Old English homily for the feast of Saint Lawrence on 10 August is the twenty-ninth piece in the First Series of the Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, compiled around 989–991. It retells the Latin legendary passion of the Roman deacon. Under the emperor Decius, Bishop Sixtus and his deacons Felicissimus and Agapetus are arrested and martyred. Lawrence then gives the church's treasure to the poor and is put to death by fire. The homily shows how Ælfric turned Latin hagiography into English prose for preaching.

This Old English homily for the feast of the Assumption on 15 August is the thirtieth item in the first series of Catholic Homilies, which Ælfric of Eynsham composed around 989–991. It draws chiefly on the Latin letter Cogitis me, addressed to Paula and Eustochium. The letter was long attributed to Jerome but is now recognised as the work of Paschasius Radbertus. Following that source, Ælfric warns against apocryphal accounts of Mary's death and is cautious about whether she was taken up bodily, while praising her virginity and heavenly glory.

This Old English homily is the thirty-first item in the first series of the Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, written around 989–991. It is meant for the feast of Saint Bartholomew on 25 August. Ælfric retells the apocryphal Latin passion of the apostle, which describes how Bartholomew preached in "the third India." His presence silences the demon in the idol Ashtaroth, he exposes the false healings that idol worship offered, he converts the local king, and he dies as a martyr. The homily shows how Ælfric adapted Latin hagiographical material for preaching in English.

This Old English sermon by Ælfric of Eynsham belongs to the first series of his Catholic Homilies, composed around 989–991. It was written for 29 August, the feast of the beheading of John the Baptist. Taking Mark's account of Herod imprisoning John for Herodias's sake as its text, the homily praises John as the greatest of those born of women. It then explains the gospel, beginning with the family of Herod: Herod the Great, his sons and Archelaus's succession. Like the rest of the series, it gave a lay audience patristic interpretation of Scripture in the vernacular.

This Old English sermon is part of the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, the Benedictine monk and homilist. The series was written around 990. The homily is for the Seventeenth Sunday after Pentecost and explains the Gospel reading from Luke 7:11–16, in which Jesus raises the widow's son at Nain. Following Bede, Ælfric reads the dead youth as the sinner and his mother as the Church. He treats the city gate as the bodily senses through which sin enters, and the raising as the sinner's spiritual resurrection through repentance.

This Old English homily for 29 September, the feast of Saint Michael the Archangel, belongs to the first series of Catholic Homilies. Ælfric of Eynsham, the Benedictine monk and homilist, wrote the series around 989–991. The homily tells the founding legend of Michael's shrine on Monte Gargano in southern Italy. A rich man's arrow turns back on him, and after a three-day fast the archangel appears to the local bishop. The homily goes on to describe the angels and Michael's role among them.

This is an Old English sermon for the twenty-first Sunday after Pentecost. It forms part of the first series of Catholic Homilies, which Ælfric of Eynsham wrote around 989–991. It explains the Gospel parable of the king who prepared a marriage feast for his son (Matthew 22:1–14). Ælfric states that he follows the exposition of Pope Gregory the Great. He reads the kingdom of heaven as the present Church, the gathering of the righteous. The king is God the Father, who joins the Church to his Son through the mystery of the Incarnation.

This Old English sermon for All Saints' Day, 1 November, is the thirty-sixth homily in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham. That series was composed around 989–991. The homily explains that the Church honours all saints on one feast because no one can know or separately commemorate each of them. Drawing on John's vision in Revelation, it discusses the saints as both angels and humans. It describes the nine unfallen orders of angels and the fall of the tenth through pride, then turns to the human saints.

This Old English homily is the thirty-seventh piece in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, compiled around 989–991. Ælfric wrote it for the feast of Clement of Rome on 23 November. It tells Clement's life as Latin legend gives it: he was a disciple of the apostle Peter and was chosen by Peter as his successor as bishop of Rome. Jews, pagans and Christians alike respected him, and the homily goes on to his exile and martyrdom. It is an example of how Ælfric turned Latin hagiography into vernacular preaching for lay listeners.

This is an Old English homily for the feast of St Andrew on 30 November. It is the thirty-eighth piece in the first series of Catholic Homilies, which Ælfric of Eynsham composed around 989–991. It explains the Gospel passage in which Christ calls the fishermen Peter and Andrew by the Sea of Galilee (Matthew 4:18–22). Ælfric reads this as Christ making the apostles "fishers of men." He also argues that Christ chose unlearned fishermen rather than philosophers so that the faith would be seen to spread by God's power and not by worldly eloquence.

This Old English sermon for the First Sunday of Advent is the thirty-ninth homily in the first series of Catholic Homilies. Ælfric of Eynsham, the Benedictine monk and homilist, wrote the series around 989–991 for preaching through the church year. He explains that the season up to midwinter is called Adventus Domini, the Lord's coming, and identifies that coming with Christ taking on human nature to redeem humankind from the devil. He discusses why the prophets are read in the liturgy at this season and sets Christ's first coming at his birth beside his second coming at the Last Judgement.

This is an Old English sermon by Ælfric of Eynsham for the Second Sunday of Advent. It is the closing homily of the first series of his Catholic Homilies, composed around 989–991. It explains the Gospel reading from Luke 21 about the signs in the sun, moon and stars that will come before the end of the world. Ælfric follows closely Gregory the Great's homily on the same passage. He urges his listeners to stop loving a world that is growing old, and he links the troubles of his own day to the coming of the Last Judgement.

This Old English preface opens the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric, a monk and mass-priest, written around 989–991. Ælfric says that Bishop Ælfheah of Winchester sent him to the minster at Cerne in King Æthelred's reign, at the request of the thegn Æthelmær. He explains that he translated the homilies from Latin because many English books contained errors, while only those who knew Latin, or read King Alfred's translations, had sound gospel teaching. He also points to the coming end of the world as a reason the English needed good instruction.

He links it to the repentance of Nineveh and retells the story of Jonah to urge penitence and prayer.

This Old English homily on the Lord's Prayer is the nineteenth item in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, the Benedictine monk and writer. The series was composed around 989 to 991. Meant for a Tuesday in Rogationtide, it first tells how Christ taught the apostles to pray. It then explains the Pater noster petition by petition, with teaching on God's fatherhood and Christians as adopted sons. It is a clear example of Ælfric's teaching aimed at lay people in their own language.

"Of the Catholic Faith" (De Fide Catholica) is an Old English homily by Ælfric of Eynsham, the twentieth item in the first series of his Catholic Homilies, composed around 989–991. It is assigned to a Wednesday, during Rogationtide, and follows directly on his sermon on the Lord's Prayer. In it Ælfric explains the Creed for lay listeners and presents the doctrine of the Trinity, drawing on Augustine. He starts from the distinction between the uncreated Creator and his creatures. The homily shows how the Benedictine reform tried to teach the basic points of faith in the vernacular.

This Old English sermon for the feast of the Ascension is the twenty-first item in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham. He compiled the series around 989–991 to provide orthodox preaching in the vernacular for the church year. The homily opens with a paraphrase of the liturgical reading from Acts 1. It retells Christ's forty days with his disciples after the resurrection, his promise of the Holy Spirit and his ascent from the Mount of Olives. It then explains the passage for a lay audience, drawing on earlier Latin patristic interpretation.

This Old English sermon for Pentecost is the twenty-second homily in the first series of the Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, written about 989–991. Ælfric explains how the feast began in the Old Testament. Israel kept Passover after the Exodus and the crossing of the Red Sea, and fifty days later God gave the Law at Sinai. He then sets this beside the Holy Spirit's descent on the apostles, as told in Acts. Like the rest of the series, it was meant to teach orthodox doctrine in English to lay listeners.

This Old English sermon is the twenty-third homily in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, written around 989–991. It was composed for the Second Sunday after Pentecost and explains the gospel parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31). Ælfric follows the exposition of Pope Gregory the Great and stresses that the rich man was condemned for meanness and pride rather than for theft. He warns against vanity in costly clothing and urges charity to the poor. The homily shows how Ælfric adapted patristic exegesis for preaching to lay audiences.

This Old English sermon by Ælfric of Eynsham is the twenty-fourth piece in the First Series of his Catholic Homilies, written around 989–991 and meant to be preached on the Fourth Sunday after Pentecost. It explains the Gospel reading from Luke 15, in which Pharisees and scribes complain that Jesus receives sinners, and he answers with the parable of the lost sheep. Ælfric openly follows Gregory the Great's interpretation. He reads the hundred sheep as angels and humankind, and the lost sheep as Adam, whom Christ came to earth to seek.

This Old English homily for the feast of the Nativity of John the Baptist on 24 June is the twenty-fifth item in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, compiled around 989–991. It explains the Gospel of Luke's account of the birth of John to Zacharias and Elizabeth and describes his ascetic life and his preaching in the wilderness. It also separates John's baptism, which did not forgive sins, from the baptism of Christ that he foretold. In this way Ælfric brought Latin patristic biblical interpretation to an English-speaking audience.

This Old English homily for the feast of Saints Peter and Paul on 29 June is the twenty-sixth item in the first series of Catholic Homilies. Ælfric of Eynsham wrote it around 989–991. It begins with an exposition of Matthew 16:13–19, which covers Peter's confession of Christ at Caesarea Philippi and the promise of the keys, drawing on Bede's commentary. It then tells the story of the two apostles' martyrdom at Rome. The homily is an example of Ælfric's effort to give lay audiences orthodox teaching in English, based on Latin patristic authorities.

This Old English homily by Ælfric of Eynsham was written for 30 June, the feast honouring the Apostle Paul. It is the twenty-seventh piece in the first series of his Catholic Homilies, composed around 989–991. The sermon retells Paul's life, drawing mainly on the Acts of the Apostles. It covers his early training in the Jewish law, his persecution of Christians and his part in Stephen's death, his conversion on the road to Damascus, and his martyrdom alongside Peter. Ælfric presents Paul as the teacher of all nations.

This Old English sermon belongs to the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, written about 989–991. It was meant to be preached on the Eleventh Sunday after Pentecost and explains the Gospel reading in which Jesus weeps over Jerusalem as he approaches the city (Luke 19:41 and following). Ælfric follows Gregory the Great's interpretation. He tells how the city's inhabitants rejected repentance, persecuted the apostles and were finally destroyed by the Romans under Vespasian. He presents that destruction as divine judgement and as a warning to the soul.

This Old English homily for the feast of Saint Lawrence on 10 August is the twenty-ninth piece in the First Series of the Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, compiled around 989–991. It retells the Latin legendary passion of the Roman deacon. Under the emperor Decius, Bishop Sixtus and his deacons Felicissimus and Agapetus are arrested and martyred. Lawrence then gives the church's treasure to the poor and is put to death by fire. The homily shows how Ælfric turned Latin hagiography into English prose for preaching.

This Old English homily for the feast of the Assumption on 15 August is the thirtieth item in the first series of Catholic Homilies, which Ælfric of Eynsham composed around 989–991. It draws chiefly on the Latin letter Cogitis me, addressed to Paula and Eustochium. The letter was long attributed to Jerome but is now recognised as the work of Paschasius Radbertus. Following that source, Ælfric warns against apocryphal accounts of Mary's death and is cautious about whether she was taken up bodily, while praising her virginity and heavenly glory.

This Old English homily is the thirty-first item in the first series of the Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, written around 989–991. It is meant for the feast of Saint Bartholomew on 25 August. Ælfric retells the apocryphal Latin passion of the apostle, which describes how Bartholomew preached in "the third India." His presence silences the demon in the idol Ashtaroth, he exposes the false healings that idol worship offered, he converts the local king, and he dies as a martyr. The homily shows how Ælfric adapted Latin hagiographical material for preaching in English.

This Old English sermon by Ælfric of Eynsham belongs to the first series of his Catholic Homilies, composed around 989–991. It was written for 29 August, the feast of the beheading of John the Baptist. Taking Mark's account of Herod imprisoning John for Herodias's sake as its text, the homily praises John as the greatest of those born of women. It then explains the gospel, beginning with the family of Herod: Herod the Great, his sons and Archelaus's succession. Like the rest of the series, it gave a lay audience patristic interpretation of Scripture in the vernacular.

This Old English sermon is part of the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, the Benedictine monk and homilist. The series was written around 990. The homily is for the Seventeenth Sunday after Pentecost and explains the Gospel reading from Luke 7:11–16, in which Jesus raises the widow's son at Nain. Following Bede, Ælfric reads the dead youth as the sinner and his mother as the Church. He treats the city gate as the bodily senses through which sin enters, and the raising as the sinner's spiritual resurrection through repentance.

This Old English homily for 29 September, the feast of Saint Michael the Archangel, belongs to the first series of Catholic Homilies. Ælfric of Eynsham, the Benedictine monk and homilist, wrote the series around 989–991. The homily tells the founding legend of Michael's shrine on Monte Gargano in southern Italy. A rich man's arrow turns back on him, and after a three-day fast the archangel appears to the local bishop. The homily goes on to describe the angels and Michael's role among them.

This is an Old English sermon for the twenty-first Sunday after Pentecost. It forms part of the first series of Catholic Homilies, which Ælfric of Eynsham wrote around 989–991. It explains the Gospel parable of the king who prepared a marriage feast for his son (Matthew 22:1–14). Ælfric states that he follows the exposition of Pope Gregory the Great. He reads the kingdom of heaven as the present Church, the gathering of the righteous. The king is God the Father, who joins the Church to his Son through the mystery of the Incarnation.

This Old English sermon for All Saints' Day, 1 November, is the thirty-sixth homily in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham. That series was composed around 989–991. The homily explains that the Church honours all saints on one feast because no one can know or separately commemorate each of them. Drawing on John's vision in Revelation, it discusses the saints as both angels and humans. It describes the nine unfallen orders of angels and the fall of the tenth through pride, then turns to the human saints.

This Old English homily is the thirty-seventh piece in the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, compiled around 989–991. Ælfric wrote it for the feast of Clement of Rome on 23 November. It tells Clement's life as Latin legend gives it: he was a disciple of the apostle Peter and was chosen by Peter as his successor as bishop of Rome. Jews, pagans and Christians alike respected him, and the homily goes on to his exile and martyrdom. It is an example of how Ælfric turned Latin hagiography into vernacular preaching for lay listeners.

This is an Old English homily for the feast of St Andrew on 30 November. It is the thirty-eighth piece in the first series of Catholic Homilies, which Ælfric of Eynsham composed around 989–991. It explains the Gospel passage in which Christ calls the fishermen Peter and Andrew by the Sea of Galilee (Matthew 4:18–22). Ælfric reads this as Christ making the apostles "fishers of men." He also argues that Christ chose unlearned fishermen rather than philosophers so that the faith would be seen to spread by God's power and not by worldly eloquence.

This Old English sermon for the First Sunday of Advent is the thirty-ninth homily in the first series of Catholic Homilies. Ælfric of Eynsham, the Benedictine monk and homilist, wrote the series around 989–991 for preaching through the church year. He explains that the season up to midwinter is called Adventus Domini, the Lord's coming, and identifies that coming with Christ taking on human nature to redeem humankind from the devil. He discusses why the prophets are read in the liturgy at this season and sets Christ's first coming at his birth beside his second coming at the Last Judgement.

This is an Old English sermon by Ælfric of Eynsham for the Second Sunday of Advent. It is the closing homily of the first series of his Catholic Homilies, composed around 989–991. It explains the Gospel reading from Luke 21 about the signs in the sun, moon and stars that will come before the end of the world. Ælfric follows closely Gregory the Great's homily on the same passage. He urges his listeners to stop loving a world that is growing old, and he links the troubles of his own day to the coming of the Last Judgement.

This Old English preface opens the first series of Catholic Homilies by Ælfric, a monk and mass-priest, written around 989–991. Ælfric says that Bishop Ælfheah of Winchester sent him to the minster at Cerne in King Æthelred's reign, at the request of the thegn Æthelmær. He explains that he translated the homilies from Latin because many English books contained errors, while only those who knew Latin, or read King Alfred's translations, had sound gospel teaching. He also points to the coming end of the world as a reason the English needed good instruction.

This Latin preface opens the first series of the Catholic Homilies by Ælfric of Eynsham, written around 990. Calling himself a pupil of Bishop Æthelwold, Ælfric addresses Archbishop Sigeric of Canterbury. He explains that he has put Latin teaching into plain English, translating sense for sense, so that the unlearned can understand it. He names his authorities: Augustine, Jerome, Bede, Gregory, Smaragdus and Haymo. He describes the forty sermons, which cover Gospel readings and saints' lives, announces a second volume and suggests that the two be read in church in alternate years.

The Acts of Paul and Thecla is an anonymous apocryphal narrative, originally written in Greek in the second century as part of the larger Acts of Paul. It also circulated on its own, and versions survive in Syriac and other languages. It tells how Thecla, a young woman of Iconium, hears Paul preach on chastity, breaks off her engagement, and survives two attempts to execute her before becoming an itinerant teacher. The text includes a well-known physical description of Paul and was the foundation of Thecla's widespread cult.

The Acts of Peter and Andrew is an anonymous apocryphal narrative about the apostles. It continues the Acts of Andrew and Matthias: after his mission in the city of the man-eaters, Andrew is carried by a cloud to rejoin Peter, Matthew and Alexander. Christ, appearing as a child, sends the apostles to preach in a city of barbarians. There Peter makes a camel pass through the eye of a needle, and a rich man named Onesiphorus is converted. The text survives in Greek and other versions. Its date is uncertain but is usually placed in late antiquity or the early Middle Ages.

This anonymous Greek apocryphal narrative is sometimes attributed to Marcellus, a supposed disciple of Peter, and is often called the Pseudo-Marcellus Acts. Its date is uncertain, but it is usually placed in late antiquity. It describes Paul's arrival in Rome despite Jewish opposition and his reconciliation with Peter. The two apostles then confront Simon Magus before the emperor Nero, and Simon falls to his death. The story ends with the martyrdom of both apostles: Peter is crucified upside down and Paul is beheaded. The text shaped later tradition about the apostles' shared mission and death in Rome.

The Genuine Acts of Peter is an anonymous hagiographical passion of Peter, archbishop of Alexandria, who was martyred in 311 during the persecution under Maximinus Daia. Written in a florid panegyric style, it tells how Peter rose to the episcopate, opposed pagans and heretics, and cut Arius off from the Church before being beheaded. It includes the well-known vision of Christ in a torn garment, which is blamed on Arius. The date of composition is uncertain. The text survives in Latin and is probably based on Greek tradition.

The Apocalypse of Peter is an anonymous early Christian apocalypse, probably written in Greek in the first half of the second century. It falsely claims Peter as its author. In it the risen Christ shows the apostles visions of the glorified righteous and of the punishments of the damned. Sinners suffer torments that match their sins. It is the earliest surviving Christian work to describe heaven and hell in detail. The Muratorian fragment names it, though with reservations. It shaped later visions of the afterlife and survives in a shorter Greek version and a longer Ethiopic one.

The Apocalypse of the Holy Mother of God is an anonymous Byzantine apocryphal apocalypse written in Greek. It is usually dated between the ninth and eleventh centuries, though the date is uncertain. After praying on the Mount of Olives, the Virgin Mary is led by the archangel Michael on a tour of the punishments of sinners in hell. Moved by their suffering, she intercedes for them, and the damned are granted a yearly respite from Easter to Pentecost. Drawing on the Apocalypse of Paul, the work was widely popular and survives in many manuscripts and translations, notably into Slavonic.

These are passages from a lost Greek treatise against Montanism by Apollonius, an ecclesiastical writer probably from Asia Minor, active around 180–210. Eusebius preserved them in his Ecclesiastical History. They attack Montanus for dissolving marriages, imposing fasts, calling the Phrygian towns Pepuza and Tymion "Jerusalem," and collecting money from followers. They also accuse the prophetesses of leaving their husbands and expose the Montanists Themison and Alexander. The fragments record a tradition that Christ told the apostles to stay in Jerusalem for twelve years. Jerome praised the work, and Tertullian wrote a reply to it.

The Apology of Aristides is one of the earliest surviving Christian apologies, written by Aristides, a philosopher of Athens, in the second century. Eusebius says it was addressed to Hadrian, while the Syriac heading names Antoninus Pius. Aristides argues from the order of the cosmos to one eternal God. He then sorts humanity into groups and judges their religions, finding barbarians, Greeks and Jews in error. He praises the moral life of Christians. Long thought lost, the text was recovered in the late nineteenth century from a Syriac version and from a Greek version reworked into the romance Barlaam and Josaphat.

The Arabic Infancy Gospel is an anonymous apocryphal account of the birth and childhood of Jesus. It may go back as early as the sixth century and is closely related to the East Syriac History of the Virgin, either as a translation of it or through a shared Syriac source. It draws on the Gospel of James and the Infancy Gospel of Thomas as well as oral tradition. Presented as taken from a book of "Joseph the high priest," it recounts the nativity, the flight into Egypt and many miracles worked by the child Jesus, often with Mary's involvement.

The Paradosis Pilati, or Giving Up of Pilate, is an anonymous Greek apocryphon belonging to the Pilate cycle. It is usually dated to roughly the fifth or sixth century, though its date is uncertain. It continues the Anaphora Pilati, Pilate's report to the emperor. Caesar, enraged that the darkness and earthquake at the crucifixion had struck the whole world, summons Pilate to Rome and sentences him to death. Pilate blames the Jewish leaders, repents, and is beheaded. A heavenly voice blesses him, and an angel receives his head. The story reflects the early Christian tradition that treated Pilate favourably.

The Gospel of Nicodemus, also called the Acts of Pilate, is an anonymous apocryphal gospel that claims to come from records kept by Nicodemus. It was probably written in Greek, and its sections date from different times; the work as it survives is usually placed in the fourth or fifth century. The first part tells of Jesus' trial before Pilate, his crucifixion and his resurrection. The second part describes Christ's descent into Hell. It was widely translated, including into Latin and Coptic, and shaped medieval accounts of the Harrowing of Hell.

The Gospel according to Peter is a non-canonical gospel written in Greek and falsely attributed to the apostle Peter. It is usually dated to the second century. Only part of it survives, in a fragment found at Akhmim in Egypt in 1886–87. That fragment tells of the Passion, burial and resurrection of Jesus, and it places responsibility for the crucifixion on Herod and the Jews rather than on Pilate. It also describes Christ coming out of the tomb. Around 200, Serapion of Antioch warned against reading it because of passages he judged docetic.

The Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew is an anonymous Latin infancy gospel, usually dated to the seventh or eighth century, that tells of the birth and life of the Virgin Mary and the childhood of Jesus. Much of it adapts the Greek Gospel of James and adds an account of the Flight into Egypt. Later versions take in material from the Infancy Gospel of Thomas. In some manuscripts a preface falsely claims that Jerome translated it from a Hebrew original by Matthew the Evangelist. It was widely read in the medieval West and shaped how artists depicted the Life of Mary.

This is a modern grouping of short fragments from discourses, homilies and other writings attributed to Hippolytus of Rome, the early third-century theologian who died around 235. The full works are lost and survive only as quotations in later Christian authors and anthologies. The pieces cover the resurrection and the incorruptible nature of the risen body, the unchanging will of God, and Christ's divinity and humanity as shown in the Passion, as in a homily on the Paschal Supper. Some attributions are uncertain, as with much of the Hippolytan corpus.

The History of Joseph the Carpenter is an anonymous apocryphal narrative. It was probably composed in Greek in Byzantine Egypt, likely in the late sixth or early seventh century. Apart from a few Greek papyrus fragments, it survives in Coptic and Arabic versions. In the text Jesus tells his disciples on the Mount of Olives about Joseph's life, his marriage to Mary and his death at the age of 111, with Jesus and Mary at his side. It bears witness to belief in Mary's perpetual virginity and to the early devotion to Joseph as patron of a holy death.

A short set of spurious Latin letters falsely attributed to Ignatius of Antioch. The set has two letters from Ignatius to the apostle John, one to the Virgin Mary, and a brief reply from Mary urging him to stand firm in the faith. The first letter praises Mary's humility, patience and charity. It describes Christian women eager to visit her and question her. The letters were composed in the medieval West and their exact date is uncertain. They have no connection with the genuine Ignatius, but they reflect growing medieval devotion to Mary.

The Syriac recension is a short Syriac version of three letters attributed to Ignatius of Antioch, the bishop who wrote to churches on his way to martyrdom in Rome in the early second century. The three letters are addressed to Polycarp of Smyrna, the Ephesians and the Romans. William Cureton published it in 1845 and argued that it preserved the only authentic Ignatian text. Most scholars, following Zahn and Lightfoot, now regard it as an abridgement of the Greek middle recension of seven letters. It played a central role in nineteenth-century debates over whether the letters are genuine.

The Infancy Gospel of Thomas is an anonymous apocryphal gospel about the childhood of Jesus, generally dated to the second century and originally written in Greek. It survives in several recensions, including two Greek forms and a Latin form. In some versions it is attributed to "Thomas the Israelite". It tells of miracles the boy Jesus performed between the ages of five and twelve, such as bringing clay sparrows to life. Some show him punishing those who cross him. With the Protevangelium of James, it is among the earliest and most influential narratives of Jesus' youth.

This short apocryphal letter, preserved in Latin, claims to be from Pontius Pilate to the emperor Tiberius about the crucifixion of Jesus. Its author is unknown, and its date is uncertain. In the letter, Pilate praises Jesus as a uniquely pious man. He blames the Jewish leaders and the crowd for his death and says he gave in only because he feared a riot. He also mentions the wonders at the crucifixion and how well the disciples are doing. It belongs to the Pilate cycle, a group of writings that present Pilate as a witness to Christ's innocence.

The Martyrdom of the Holy and Glorious Apostle Bartholomew is an anonymous apocryphal account of the apostle's final mission and death. It survives in Greek and is closely related to a Latin passion; it probably dates from somewhere between the fifth and seventh centuries. It describes Bartholomew's preaching in "India", where his presence silences the demon worshipped in the temple of Astaruth. He converts King Polymius and his household, and the king's brother Astyages then has him put to death. The text is an important witness to the legends about Bartholomew that shaped his later veneration.

The Narrative of Joseph of Arimathaea is an anonymous Greek apocryphal text belonging to the literature that grew up around the Passion and Pontius Pilate. Its date is uncertain and is usually placed somewhere between late antiquity and the early Middle Ages. Joseph, who asked Pilate for Jesus' body, tells the story in the first person. He describes the crimes of the two robbers crucified with Christ, Gestas and the penitent Demas, along with his own imprisonment, and expands on the Gospel accounts of the crucifixion and its aftermath.

The Narrative of Zosimus, also known as the History of the Rechabites, is an anonymous apocryphal text that survives in Greek, Syriac and other languages. It tells of Zosimus, a desert hermit who, after forty years of strict fasting, is guided by an angel to the land of the Blessed. These are descendants of the Rechabites of Jeremiah 35, who live a sinless life apart from the world. Its date and origin are disputed. Some scholars see an early Jewish core, which was later reworked by Christians, possibly between the first and sixth centuries.

The Nicene Creed is the profession of Christian faith first adopted by the First Council of Nicaea in 325 against Arianism. It affirms that the Son is "begotten, not made" and "of one substance" (homoousios) with the Father, and it ends with anathemas against Arian formulas. According to tradition, the First Council of Constantinople expanded it in 381, mainly the article on the Holy Spirit. This Niceno-Constantinopolitan form remains the most widely shared creed among Eastern and Western churches.

The Passing of Mary is an anonymous apocryphal narrative surviving in two Latin recensions, part of the wider Transitus Mariae tradition, generally dated between the fifth and seventh centuries. It goes on to describe her burial and the bodily taking up of Mary into heaven. The second form is ascribed to Melito of Sardis, though the attribution is spurious. These texts strongly shaped later Western belief and art concerning the Dormition and Assumption.

This short anonymous Latin martyr account tells of Symphorosa, a Christian widow, and her seven sons. They are said to have been put to death at Tibur (Tivoli) under the emperor Hadrian. According to the story, pagan priests accused her when Hadrian ordered religious ceremonies for his new villa there. She refused to sacrifice to the gods and was drowned, and her sons were executed the next day. Manuscripts attribute the text to Julius Africanus, but this is doubtful. Its date is uncertain, and it is probably a later composition.

The Passion of the Scillitan Martyrs is a short anonymous Latin account of the trial of Christians from Scilli in Roman North Africa. Speratus and his companions were tried before the proconsul Saturninus at Carthage on 17 July 180 and beheaded. The text consists mostly of the court interrogation, in which the accused refuse to swear by the emperor's genius. Speratus also mentions "books and epistles of Paul." It is the earliest dated Christian document from Latin Africa and among the most reliable of the early acts of the martyrs.

This is a short letter from four Egyptian bishops, Hesychius, Pachomius, Theodorus and Phileas of Thmuis, to Meletius, bishop of Lycopolis. It was written about 305–307, while the authors were imprisoned during the Great Persecution under Diocletian. The bishops rebuke Meletius for ordaining clergy in dioceses outside his own jurisdiction. They appeal to the ancestral law of the Church, under which each bishop acts only within his own see. The letter is an early witness to the Melitian schism in Egypt. It was probably written in Greek but survives only in Latin.

This Greek letter was written by Phileas, bishop of Thmuis in Lower Egypt, to the Christians of his own city during the Great Persecution under Diocletian. Phileas wrote it while imprisoned at Alexandria, shortly before his own martyrdom around 306. The surviving passages, preserved by Eusebius of Caesarea in his Church History (Book VIII), describe the tortures suffered by the martyrs of Alexandria. They praise the martyrs' steadfastness and present it as an imitation of Christ's self-emptying. The letter is a valuable eyewitness account of the persecution in Egypt.

The Protevangelium of James is an anonymous Greek infancy gospel from the second century. It presents itself as the work of James, the brother of the Lord. It tells of the miraculous conception of Mary to Joachim and Anna and her upbringing in the Temple. It goes on to her betrothal to the elderly widower Joseph, the birth of Jesus in a cave near Bethlehem, and the events that followed. It is the earliest surviving text to assert Mary's perpetual virginity. Although the Latin West condemned it as apocryphal, it shaped Marian feasts, art and devotion, especially in the East.

The Recognitions is a fourth-century Christian romance falsely attributed to Clement of Rome. It is one of two surviving versions of the Pseudo-Clementine writings, alongside the Clementine Homilies. It tells of Clement's conversion, his travels with the apostle Peter, Peter's debates with Simon Magus, and how Clement was reunited with his scattered family. The Greek original is lost. The text survives complete in Rufinus of Aquileia's Latin translation of about 406, and in part in an early Syriac version. It is an important source for Jewish-Christian traditions.

The Exhortation to Repentance (Exhortatio de paenitentia) is a short anonymous Latin work that was long transmitted among the writings of Cyprian of Carthage. It is now counted among the Pseudo-Cyprianic texts. Its date is uncertain and is generally placed between the mid-third and fifth centuries. It is a collection of biblical testimonia, mostly from the Psalms and the Prophets, set out like Cyprian's own proof-text collections. Its stated purpose is to show that all sins may be forgiven to anyone who turns to God with his whole heart.

The Key (Clavis Scripturae) is a Latin glossary of biblical symbolism attributed to Melito of Sardis. The attribution draws on Eusebius, who lists a work by Melito called "The Key", but that work is lost. The surviving Latin text is generally regarded as a later medieval compilation, probably from the early Middle Ages, though its exact date is uncertain. It is arranged by subject. Each entry takes a scriptural term, such as the head, eyes or right hand of the Lord, gives its spiritual or allegorical meaning, and supports it with biblical quotations.

This apologetic discourse survives in Syriac and is presented as an address by Melito, the second-century bishop of Sardis, to "Antoninus Caesar." Scholars generally regard it as pseudonymous and distinct from Melito's lost Greek apology to Marcus Aurelius. Its date and original language are uncertain, though it is usually placed in the late second or third century. The speaker urges the emperor to turn from error to the knowledge of the one true God. He attacks idolatry and explains pagan deities as deified human beings. It is an important witness to early Syriac Christian apologetic.

A Strain of the Judgment of the Lord (Carmen de judicio Domini) is an anonymous Latin poem in hexameters. It has been handed down among the works wrongly attributed to Tertullian, and its real author and date are unknown. It is generally placed somewhere between the fourth and sixth centuries. The poem opens with a classical appeal to the Muses and goes on to praise God as Creator of nature and humanity. It then turns to death, the resurrection and the final judgment, with the rewards of the righteous and the punishment of the wicked.

The Carmen adversus Marcionitas is an anonymous Latin poem in five books of hexameters against the teachings of Marcion and his followers. It was long transmitted among the works of Tertullian but is not by him. Its author and date are uncertain: it is usually placed between the fourth and fifth centuries, and some scholars have suggested Commodian. The poem defends the unity of God, the resurrection of the flesh and the harmony of the Old and New Testaments. It also gives a list of the early bishops of Rome.

The Report of Pilate (Anaphora Pilati) is an anonymous Greek apocryphon from the Pilate cycle, preserved in two forms and usually dated, uncertainly, to the fourth or fifth century. It is presented as a letter from Pontius Pilate to the emperor in Rome, describing the miracles of Jesus, his trial and crucifixion at the demand of the Jews, the darkness and earthquake that followed, and his resurrection. It often circulates with the Acts of Pilate and the Paradosis Pilati. Together these texts reflect a growing early Christian tradition that presented Pilate as a reluctant witness to Christ.

The Apocalypse of Paul, also called the Visio Pauli, is an anonymous apocryphal apocalypse probably written in Greek in the late fourth century. It claims to be a revelation found under Paul's house in Tarsus in the reign of Theodosius. It expands on 2 Corinthians 12 and tells of the apostle's journey through heaven and hell, describing the judgment of souls and the rewards and punishments that follow. The Greek original survives only in part. Through Latin and other versions it became widely read and shaped medieval ideas of the afterlife.

Rufinus of Aquileia wrote this Latin preface around 397–398 for his translation of Origen's treatise On First Principles (Peri Archon). In it he places his work in a line of Latin translations of Origen. He praises, without naming him, a "brother and colleague", clearly Jerome, who had translated Origen's homilies on the Song of Songs for Pope Damasus. He also explains that he altered or left out passages he thought heretics had added to the text. Because he invoked Jerome's earlier praise of Origen, the preface set off the bitter quarrel between the two men over Origen.

The Diatessaron is a gospel harmony made by Tatian, a second-century Christian apologist and ascetic from the Syriac-speaking East, around 160–175. It weaves Matthew, Mark, Luke and John into a single continuous story of Jesus's life, opening with the prologue of John. Scholars disagree on whether Tatian first wrote it in Syriac or Greek. It was the standard gospel text in Syriac churches until the fifth century, when the separate gospels replaced it. The original is lost and is known through later translations and commentaries, including a medieval Arabic version.

This is a collection of passages from lost writings of Tatian, the second-century Syrian Christian apologist known for the Address to the Greeks and the Diatessaron. The passages survive only as quotations in later authors such as Clement of Alexandria and Jerome. They include lines from his treatise On Perfection according to the Saviour, which presents marriage as an obstacle to prayer. Jerome's reports call Tatian a leader of the Encratites who condemned all sexual union and held that Christ's flesh was only apparent. The fragments are important evidence for the strict ascetic views of Tatian's later years.

The Apocalypse of Paul, known in Latin as the Visio Pauli, is an anonymous apocryphal apocalypse probably written in Greek in the late fourth century. It builds on Paul's rapture to the third heaven in 2 Corinthians 12 and describes his guided tour of heaven and hell, the judgement of souls at death, and the punishment of sinners, including unworthy clergy and monks. A prologue claims it was found in Paul's house at Tarsus under Theodosius. Latin, Syriac and other versions made it widely read in the Middle Ages, and Dante probably knew it.

The Badarak (Classical Armenian Patarag, "offering") is the eucharistic liturgy of the Armenian Church. It is anonymous and grew over several centuries. Tradition links its beginnings to Gregory the Illuminator and Nerses the Great, and its fuller arrangement to the fifth-century scholars who translated the Bible into Armenian. It draws on Cappadocian and Byzantine models, including the liturgies associated with Basil and John Chrysostom, and its anaphora bears the name of Athanasius. Its exact date of composition is uncertain. It is still the central act of worship in Armenian Christianity.

1 Chronicles is the first half of the Book of Chronicles, a Hebrew scriptural history that the Septuagint divided into two books and called Paralipomenon. Tradition ascribed it to Ezra. Modern scholars instead attribute it to an anonymous priestly author, "the Chronicler," writing in Jerusalem in the Persian or early Hellenistic period. It opens with genealogies from Adam to the exiles who returned from Babylon. It then narrates the death of Saul and the reign of David, stressing the ark, the Levites and the preparations for the Temple.

The First Epistle to the Corinthians is a letter of the New Testament written in Greek by the apostle Paul, with Sosthenes named as co-sender, to the church he had founded at Corinth. It was probably written from Ephesus around 53–57. Paul responds to reports of factions and to questions from the community about sexual morality, marriage, food offered to idols, conduct in worship, the Lord's Supper and spiritual gifts. It includes the celebrated hymn to love (chapter 13) and the earliest extended teaching on the resurrection (chapter 15).

1 Esdras, also called Greek Esdras or 3 Esdras (its Vulgate title), is an anonymous book of the Septuagint. It retells material found in 2 Chronicles 35–36, Ezra and part of Nehemiah: from Josiah's Passover, through the return from exile and the rebuilding of the Temple, to Ezra's reading of the Law. Its best-known addition is the contest of three guards at the court of Darius, which Zerubbabel wins. It is probably of the second century BC. Eastern churches accept it as canonical, but in the West it is counted among the apocrypha.

The First Epistle of John is a New Testament writing in Greek, the first of the three Johannine epistles. It names no author. Tradition attributes it to John the Apostle, but its authorship is disputed, and many scholars place it within the Johannine community around 85–100. It reads more like a homily than a letter. It teaches that God is light and God is love, and that believers must confess their sins and love one another. It also rejects those who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. Its theology of love and fellowship has strongly shaped Christian thought.

1 Kings is the first half of the Book of Kings in the Hebrew Bible. The Septuagint and Vulgate tradition calls it 3 Kingdoms (Regnorum III). The anonymous work belongs to the Deuteronomistic history. Scholars generally date a first edition to the late seventh century BC and a final edition to the mid-sixth. It tells of David's death and Solomon's accession and reign, including the building of the Jerusalem Temple. It then covers the division of the kingdom under Rehoboam and Jeroboam and the later kings of Israel and Judah, ending with Elijah's conflict with Ahab.

1 Maccabees is an anonymous historical book, probably written in Hebrew in the Hasmonean kingdom in the late second century BC. The Hebrew original is lost, and the book survives in the Greek of the Septuagint. It begins with Alexander the Great's conquests and goes on to tell of Antiochus IV Epiphanes' decrees against Jewish practice and the revolt led by Mattathias and his sons, chiefly Judas Maccabeus. It ends with Simon as high priest, about 134 BC. Catholic and Orthodox churches accept it as deuterocanonical scripture, but it is not part of the Hebrew Bible.

The First Epistle of Peter is a letter in the New Testament, one of the Catholic Epistles. Its author presents himself as the apostle Peter, writing from "Babylon", probably meaning Rome. Many scholars, however, think it came from a Roman Christian circle linked to Peter, sometime around 60–90. It is addressed to Christians scattered across Asia Minor who were suffering persecution. The letter urges them to keep hope, holiness and patient endurance, modelled on the sufferings of Christ. It also gives household instructions and contains a famous passage on Christ preaching to the "spirits in prison".

1 Samuel is the first half of the Book of Samuel in the Hebrew Bible. The Septuagint calls it 1 Kingdoms and the Vulgate 1 Kings. It is anonymous. Jewish tradition credits it to the prophet Samuel, with additions by Gad and Nathan. Modern scholars see it as part of the Deuteronomistic history, put together from older sources around the seventh to sixth centuries BC. It tells of Samuel's birth to Hannah and his career as a prophet, the fortunes of the Ark of the Covenant, Saul's anointing and rejection as Israel's first king, and David's rise.

The First Epistle to the Thessalonians is a letter of the New Testament sent by the apostle Paul, together with Silvanus and Timothy, to the Christian community he had founded at Thessalonica in Macedonia. It was probably written around 50–52, most likely from Corinth. Scholars widely accept it as authentic, and it is often regarded as the earliest surviving Christian writing. Paul gives thanks for the converts' faith under persecution and defends his own conduct among them. He urges them to live holy lives and addresses the fate of believers who have died before the Lord's return.

The First Epistle to Timothy is a New Testament letter written in Greek and addressed by the apostle Paul to his co-worker Timothy, who had been left at Ephesus. With 2 Timothy and Titus it forms the Pastoral Epistles. It warns against false teachers, gives directions on prayer and worship, and sets out qualifications for bishops and deacons and rules on widows and elders. Pauline authorship is disputed. Many scholars date it to the late first or early second century. It was important for later teaching on church order and ministry.

2 Chronicles is the second half of the Book of Chronicles in the Hebrew Bible, which was divided into two books in the Septuagint. Greek and Latin tradition calls it Paralipomenon. It is anonymous. Tradition credited it to Ezra, but scholars attribute it to an unknown "Chronicler" writing in the Persian or early Hellenistic period. It tells the story of Solomon's reign and the building of the Temple, then follows the kings of Judah to the Babylonian exile. It ends with the edict of Cyrus allowing the exiles to return.

The Second Epistle to the Corinthians is a New Testament letter written in Greek by the apostle Paul, with Timothy named as co-sender. It is addressed to the church at Corinth and the Christians of Achaia, and is usually dated about 55–57. Paul writes about comfort in suffering and defends his apostolic ministry. He also urges a collection for the church in Jerusalem and confronts rival "super-apostles." Many scholars think it combines parts of several letters. It was translated early into Syriac, Latin, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian and Georgian.

The Second Epistle of John is a short New Testament letter. Its author calls himself "the elder" and writes to "the elect lady and her children", which most readers take to mean a local church. Tradition ascribes it to the apostle John, but the authorship is disputed. It is usually dated to the late first century. The letter urges mutual love and obedience to the commandments. It warns against deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh and forbids welcoming them.

2 Kings is the second half of the Book of Kings in the Hebrew Bible. In the Septuagint and later Greek and Latin tradition it is called 4 Kingdoms. The anonymous work closes the Deuteronomistic history. It runs from Elijah's last days and Elisha's ministry through the fall of Samaria to Assyria and the reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah. It ends with the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem and Jehoiachin's release in exile. Scholars generally date a first edition to the late seventh century BC and a final edition to the mid-sixth.

2 Maccabees is an anonymous Jewish history written in Koine Greek, probably in Hellenistic Egypt in the late second century BC. It presents itself as an abridgement of a five-volume work by Jason of Cyrene. Two prefatory letters urge Egyptian Jews to keep the feast of the Temple's purification. The book then tells of the persecution under Antiochus IV Epiphanes and the revolt of Judas Maccabeus, ending with Nicanor's defeat in 161 BC. Its martyr stories, and its teaching on resurrection and prayer for the dead, influenced Christian thought. It is deuterocanonical in Catholic and Orthodox churches.

The Second Epistle of Peter is a short letter in the New Testament. Its author presents himself as the apostle Simon Peter, but most modern scholars consider it pseudonymous and date it to roughly 80–120, which may make it the latest New Testament book. It urges believers to grow in virtue and become "partakers of the divine nature," warns against false teachers, and defends the expectation of Christ's return. It overlaps closely with the Epistle of Jude, and its place in the canon was disputed in the early Church.

2 Samuel is the second half of the Book of Samuel in the Hebrew Bible. The Septuagint and Vulgate count it as the second Book of Kingdoms or Kings. It tells of David's reign, from his lament for Saul and Jonathan to his rule over Judah and Israel, his capture of Jerusalem, God's promise of a lasting dynasty, his sin with Bathsheba, and Absalom's revolt. Jewish tradition credits it to Samuel, Gad and Nathan. Modern scholars treat it as part of the Deuteronomistic history, compiled about 630–540 BC from older sources.

The Second Epistle to the Thessalonians is a short letter of the New Testament. It names Paul, Silvanus and Timothy as its senders and is addressed to the Christian community at Thessalonica in Macedonia. It encourages believers suffering persecution and promises God's just judgement when the Lord Jesus is revealed. It corrects the claim that the day of the Lord has already come, describing a "man of lawlessness" who must appear first. It also warns against idleness. Scholars disagree about whether Paul wrote it. Dates proposed range from about 50 to near the end of the first century.

The Second Epistle to Timothy is a New Testament letter. It is one of the three Pastoral Epistles and is presented as written by the apostle Paul to his co-worker Timothy. Many scholars think it was written by a later follower of Paul in the late first century, while others accept that Paul wrote it during his final imprisonment in Rome. It is framed as Paul's last charge: Timothy should endure hardship, guard sound teaching and resist false teachers. It contains the statement that all Scripture is inspired by God, and Paul's farewell, "I have fought the good fight."

The Third Epistle of John is the shortest book of the New Testament. It is a private letter from an author who calls himself "the elder" to a Christian named Gaius. Tradition attributes it to John the Apostle, but its authorship is debated, and it is usually dated to the late first century. The elder praises Gaius for welcoming travelling missionaries and condemns Diotrephes for refusing to receive them and for seeking preeminence. He also recommends Demetrius. The letter sheds rare light on authority and hospitality in the early church. Some early churches questioned whether it belonged in the canon.

3 Maccabees is an anonymous Jewish work composed in Koine Greek, probably in Egypt during the first century BC. Despite its title, it has nothing to do with the Maccabean Revolt. It tells how Ptolemy IV Philopator, after his victory at Raphia, was prevented by divine power from entering the Jerusalem Temple. He then turned against the Jews of Egypt and ordered them trampled by elephants, but God delivered them, and a festival was founded in thanksgiving. The book is regarded as scripture in the Eastern Orthodox, Armenian and Syriac churches.

The Acts of the Apostles is the fifth book of the New Testament. It forms the second half of a two-volume work with the Gospel of Luke and is addressed, like that Gospel, to Theophilus. Tradition names Luke, a companion of Paul, as its author, though scholars disagree about this; it is usually dated around 80–90. Acts begins with Christ's ascension and Pentecost and describes the early Jerusalem church. It then follows the spread of the gospel to the Gentiles, mostly through Paul's missionary journeys, and ends with his imprisonment in Rome.

Amos is a prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It is the third of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew order and the second in the Septuagint. It is attributed to Amos, a herdsman from Tekoa in Judah. He preached in the northern kingdom of Israel around 760–750 BC, under Jeroboam II and Uzziah. Its nine chapters announce oracles against the surrounding nations and then against Israel itself. They condemn oppression of the poor, empty worship and injustice. Scholars debate how much of the book's account of the prophet is historical.

The Book of Baruch is a short book of Jewish scripture attributed to Baruch son of Neriah, the scribe of the prophet Jeremiah. Its real author is anonymous, and scholars date it to roughly the second century BC. It is set among the Babylonian exiles and contains a confession of sin, a poem in praise of wisdom identified with the Law, and words of comfort to Jerusalem. It survives in Greek, though parts may have been translated from Hebrew. Part of the Septuagint, it is canonical for Catholic and Orthodox Christians but counted among the Apocrypha by Jews and Protestants.

The Epistle to the Colossians is a New Testament letter addressed to the Christian community at Colossae in Phrygia, Asia Minor. It names Paul and Timothy as senders, but many scholars doubt that Paul wrote it, and its date is uncertain. It is usually placed between about 58 and 80. The letter presents Christ as supreme over all creation and powers. It warns against a local "philosophy" involving ascetic and ritual practices and gives instructions for Christian households. Its close parallels with Ephesians have long attracted scholarly attention.

The Book of Daniel is a biblical apocalypse set during the Babylonian exile in the 6th century BC. Most scholars date its final form to about 167–163 BC, during the persecution under Antiochus IV Epiphanes. Its six court tales (chapters 1–6), written mostly in Aramaic, tell of Daniel and his companions at the Babylonian and Persian courts. Four visions follow (chapters 7–12), written mainly in Hebrew. The Greek versions, the Old Greek and Theodotion, add Susanna, Bel and the Dragon, and the Prayer of Azariah. Daniel strongly shaped Jewish and Christian apocalyptic thought.

Deuteronomy, the fifth book of the Torah and of the Christian Old Testament, is called Devarim ("words") in Hebrew. Its Greek name means "second law." Most of it is presented as three speeches given by Moses to Israel on the plains of Moab just before they entered the Promised Land. These speeches retell the wilderness wanderings and restate God's law. The book ends with the Song and Blessing of Moses and his death on Mount Nebo. Tradition credits it to Moses, but modern scholars generally date it to the seventh to fifth centuries BC. It contains the Shema (6:4), which Jesus quoted.

Ecclesiastes (Hebrew Qoheleth, "the Preacher" or "Teacher") is a book of wisdom literature in the Ketuvim of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. Tradition attributes it to Solomon, but most scholars date it to roughly the fifth to second centuries BC, partly because of its late Hebrew and Persian loanwords. Its speaker reflects on how fleeting and "vain" human toil, wisdom and pleasure are "under the sun," since death comes to all. He recommends enjoying life's simple gifts from God, and the book closes by urging the reader to fear God and keep his commandments.

The Epistle to the Ephesians is a New Testament letter written in Greek and addressed under the name of the apostle Paul to Christians at Ephesus. The words "at Ephesus" are missing from some early manuscripts. Many scholars think a later disciple wrote it, perhaps around 80–90, while others hold that Paul wrote it during his imprisonment around 60–62. Its main themes are God's eternal plan to unite all things in Christ, the Church as Christ's body, and the reconciliation of Jews and Gentiles. It ends with moral teaching, including household codes and the image of the "armour of God."

Esther is an anonymous book of the Hebrew Bible, one of the Five Scrolls (Megillot) among the Writings, and part of the Christian Old Testament. Its date is uncertain, usually placed in the Persian or early Hellenistic period. Set at the court of the Persian king Ahasuerus, it tells how the Jewish queen Esther and her cousin Mordecai foil Haman's plot to destroy the Jews, and it explains the origin of the festival of Purim. The Hebrew text never names God explicitly. The Greek version adds several passages, including prayers, that are accepted as canonical in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

Exodus is the second book of the Bible and of the Pentateuch. Tradition ascribes it to Moses, but modern scholars think it took shape from earlier sources and oral traditions during and after the Babylonian exile, with final revision in the Persian period. It tells how the Israelites were enslaved in Egypt and freed under Moses. It goes on to describe the covenant and the giving of the Law at Mount Sinai, and the building of the Tabernacle. Passover and the crossing of the Red Sea became central images for Jewish and Christian interpreters alike.

The Book of Ezekiel is a prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It follows Isaiah and Jeremiah among the major prophets. It presents itself as the visions and oracles of Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, dated between about 593 and 571 BC, though its final form reflects a longer process of composition. It has three main parts: judgment on Israel, oracles against the nations and promises of restoration. These include the valley of dry bones and the new Temple. Its throne-chariot vision shaped later Jewish mysticism and Christian apocalyptic and exegetical tradition.

The Book of Ezra is a book of the Hebrew Bible and Christian Old Testament, written in Hebrew and Aramaic and originally joined with Nehemiah as a single work. Its author is unknown; tradition credits Ezra himself. It tells how Cyrus allowed the exiles to return from Babylon in 538 BC and how the Temple in Jerusalem was rebuilt and dedicated in 515 BC. It then follows the scribe and priest Ezra's mission to reform the community, including his campaign against marriages with non-Jews.

The Epistle to the Galatians is a letter of the apostle Paul to the churches of Galatia in Asia Minor, written in Greek around the middle of the first century. Its exact date and the location of its recipients are disputed. Paul defends his apostolic authority and his gospel against teachers who urged Gentile converts to be circumcised and keep the Mosaic law. He argues that people are justified through faith in Christ, not works of the law. A central text for Christian ideas of grace and freedom, it was translated early into Syriac, Latin, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian and Georgian.

Genesis is the first book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament, and the opening book of the Torah, or Pentateuch. Tradition names Moses as its author. Most modern scholars instead see it as an anonymous composite work that took its final form during or after the Babylonian exile, perhaps in the fifth century BC. Its first part (chapters 1–11) tells of the creation, the fall, the flood and the early history of humanity. Its second part (chapters 12–50) follows the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph.
